newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOF says will fully support NCB restructuring plan.
newsitem.headline: MOF says will fully support NCB restructuring plan.

text.p: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) will fully support the drastic restructuring plan Nippon Credit Bank is currently drawing up, a MOF official said on Thursday.
"We have heard that NCB is in the middle of drawing up a drastic restructuring plan," said the official.
"We will, along with the BOJ, fully support its efforts," he added.
Asked whether the ministry was aware of the details of the plan as reported by the media, the official said: "I am not in a position to comment on such reports."
But he said NCB was still in the process of drawing up the plan and added that the ministry had not heard about details of the process.
The Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported on Thursday that NCB may withdraw from overseas operations under a two-stage restructuring plan currently being worked out.
An NCB spokesman said the bank was considering various measures, but added he could not specifically comment on the report.
Without citing a source, the report said that in the first stage of the plan, the bank would dispose of about 250 billion yen in problem loans in the fiscal year ending on March 31.

The disposal would be partly offset by the sale of the bank's Tokyo headquarters and its Osaka branch office for 60 billion yen, and also by parent operating profits of about 150 billion yen in 1996/97, the report said.

The newspaper said the bank planned to sell 200 to 300 billion yen worth of healthy loans to other major commercial banks in 1996/97 to help maintain a minimum international capital adequacy ratio of eight percent.
The banks have in general agreed to purchase NCB's loans, the report added.
In the second stage of the plan in 1997/98, the bank plans to close its six branches and eight subsidiaries abroad and dispose of problem loans held by troubled non-bank affiliates, it added.
By withdrawing from overseas business, NCB will not need to meet international capital adequacy requirements, it said.
